claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase high-entropy nanoalloy structure.
Nanoscale lattice strain arises from atomic-size mismatches in the nanoalloy.
The combination of configurational entropy and nanoscale lattice strain limits atomic diffusion.
Configurational entropy and lattice strain govern both structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
The as-synthesized nanoalloy has a uniform, randomly mixed, single-phase lattice.
Annealing at 800–1000°C is in a regime where enhanced diffusion typically promotes phase segregation.
A controlled inert atmosphere avoids extrinsic oxidation during annealing.
A uniformly random atomic distribution increases the energy barrier for diffusion.
High mixing entropy lowers the free energy of the single-phase state.
Nanoscale lattice strain increases activation energies for atomic hopping.
Lower single-phase free energy and increased hopping barriers jointly retard phase segregation and chemical diffusion at elevated temperature.
After identical annealing, the randomly mixed high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a single-phase microstructure better than a compositionally similar ordered or segregation-prone control.
After identical annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less elemental diffusion than the lower-entropy control.
Partial chemical ordering at fixed overall composition provides a lower-configurational-entropy control.
The predicted stabilization holds only below a temperature threshold at which thermally activated diffusion overcomes entropic stabilization.
Reactive gases such as oxygen can cause behavior outside the prediction.
Grain size, elemental ratios, and processing history may influence stability.
Failure to observe significantly less phase segregation or slower diffusion in the random high-entropy sample than in the ordered control would falsify the hypothesis.
